ICAP states that DR Congo adopted DHIS2 in 2013 as the national electronic platform for health data collection, processing and dissemination, used by Ministry of Health programmes such as the PNLS.

ICAP's support to the Ministry of Health's PNLS on HIV strategic information in the national DHIS2, including the HIV Insight Dashboard, has run since 2022 on PEPFAR funding through US CDC; no domestic funding is mentioned (dated to the document's publication).

In February 2026 Lualaba became the first province to make the HIV Insight Dashboard, an analysis application ICAP built inside the national DHIS2, the primary tool for provincial meetings and data validation; training of trainers for 112 managers from the 26 provinces was planned.

DHIS2.org states that DR Congo has used DHIS2 as a national-scale health management information system since 2013, for programme planning and management at zonal, provincial and national levels, and calls it locally owned and managed infrastructure of the Ministry of Health (dated to the document's publication).

DHIS2.org states that the national DHIS2 has been supported by funders such as Gavi, the Global Fund and US CDC, with HISP, RTI and MEASURE Evaluation as technical partners; no domestic budget line is mentioned (dated to the document's publication).

The Ministry of Public Health's national health informatics plan for 2020-2024 (PNDIS II), validated in Kinshasa on 6 August 2020, states that DHIS2 has been adopted as the country software of the national health information system (SNIS) and is being implemented progressively, and sets a complete and timely SNIS as an objective; the plan's period ends in 2024.

PNDIS II, produced by the Ministry of Public Health and its agency ANICiiS, presents the SNIS and its DHIS2 software as the ministry's own system, regulated by a normative framework of 12 sub-systems of which the primary health care component is said to be largely functional.

On 16 June 2026 the Ministry of Public Health's agency ANICNS opened call ANICNS/AMI/001/SIH/2026 for the now-mandatory approval of hospital information systems under a ministerial order of 11 March 2025; each must include a complete computerised patient record, admission on the national health identifier and FHIR/DICOM interoperability, with submissions due by 12 July 2026 and approved products to be listed in a national register.

ACP reported on 13 February 2025 that ANICNS handed the Kasaï-Oriental provincial health division 516 computers, 206 tablets and 206 routers to equip 206 care establishments, which its director general said would allow an ANICNS-approved hospital information system to be put into service and the computerised patient record to be portable; the system is described as to come, not as running.

A University of Kananga survey of 86 staff in 7 hospitals of the city of Kananga (the provincial hospital and six general referral hospitals), covering January to December 2023, found 4 respondents (4.7%) managing patient information electronically against 46 (53.5%) on forms, 20 (23.3%) on paper, 10 (11.6%) in registers and 6 (7.0%) otherwise; the authors call computerisation of patient files in the city almost non-existent, and 69 (80.2%) gave lack of means as the reason for not using software.

The Ministry of Public Health's Countdown to 2030 analysis report, signed 14 August 2022, states that the DHIS2 database lists 16,010 health facilities of which 12,050 report in DHIS2 (7,046 public, 2,596 private, 1,699 faith-based, 709 unclassified), the remaining 25% being private facilities that do not; this is a share of all health facilities whose monthly reports are in DHIS2, not of primary clinics, and the report does not say who keys them; it gives completeness of expected monthly facility reports as 84% in 2017 rising to 96% in 2020 and 2021.

A HISP evaluation that visited 5 health zones in Kinshasa and Haut-Katanga in the last quarter of 2021 states that facilities send their reports on paper to the health zone office, where they are entered into the SNIS, the national DHIS2 platform; decentralised entry exists in some large facilities with reliable power and internet, but most entry is done centrally in the health zones and most facilities have no access to the platform.

The HISP evaluation of late 2021 states that MEASURE Evaluation had funded laptops and monthly internet fees for facility-based data entry in 63 health facilities in Kikula and Kapolowe, which worked for about two years until the project's recent closure, after which the funding stopped and the devices deteriorated without replacement or maintenance; the closure is not dated beyond 'recent'.

The HISP evaluation of late 2021 places the national DHIS2-based HMIS, in place at national scale since 2013, with the HMIS division of the Ministry of Health, which it says faces fluctuating funding and organisational fragmentation, and names Gavi, the Global Fund, USAID, CDC and MEASURE Evaluation as supporting partners alongside the government.

The Sud-Kivu provincial health division's report for the fourth quarter of 2021 states that facilities transmit their reports to the health zone central office (BCZ) for keying into DHIS2 across the province's 34 health zones, and that zone teams in the 16 zones without 3G coverage had to travel to covered areas to key data before 17 VSAT links were reactivated.

The Sud-Kivu report of December 2021 lists paper collection and transmission forms supplied for health centres and health posts (CS/PS), general referral hospitals (HGR) and zone offices (BCZ), and DHIS2 data sets for basic services, secondary services, facility stock (SIGL FOSA) and hospital services in all 34 health zones; these tiers report on paper and the zone office keys the data.

The Sud-Kivu report states that from mid-July 2021 a strike by nurses and administrative staff across the province stopped reports being transmitted to the zone offices for keying into DHIS2, so provincial completeness fell to 63% in October and 41% in November 2021 for basic services, and to 44% and 34% for hospital services, against a target of 93% or more; data quality could not be assessed.

The Sud-Kivu report of December 2021 states that the Global Fund equipped the 34 health zones for internet connection in 2017 but that, for lack of funds for subscriptions, the connection lasted one semester; that PROSANI+, GIZ and MEASURE Evaluation then supplied modems and credit until they withdrew; and that in 2021 PROSANI USAID and MEASURE Malaria fund the VSAT links, reporting forms and review meetings, other partners having failed to meet their commitments on forms; no domestic funding is mentioned.

The Sud-Kivu report of December 2021, issued by the provincial health division of the Ministry of Public Health, states that the ministry's SNIS directorate (D-SNIS), with the ministry's stakeholders, mobilises the means to keep DHIS2 working, the provincial division acting as regulator in the province.

A malaria-programme support mission to the Kananga and Ndesha health zones (Kasaï Central), 15 to 18 October 2021, reports that facilities fill paper SNIS forms and monthly activity reports and transfer them to the zone central office, where data are keyed into DHIS2: it found late keying in Ndesha, DHIS2 figures that disagreed with the paper forms, a data-entry plan assigned to the zone's chief medical officer and nurse supervisor, and an internet fault at the Kananga zone office that delayed downloading the data.

The SNIS division's feedback to the 26 provincial health divisions on second-quarter 2020 data states that the SNIS was in the third year of its Plan de Renforcement du SNIS 2018-2020, whose financing remained partial, and that programmes (EPI, HIV, TB, malaria sentinel sites, nutrition, facility stock) had been integrated into DHIS2 by a modular approach.

The SNIS division's table extracted on 28 August 2020 gives, for the second quarter of 2020, 52,625 basic-services reports in DHIS2 of 53,736 expected (97.9%), 47,408 of 49,377 secondary-services reports (96%) and 5,648 of 6,249 hospital-service reports (90.4%), with overall completeness across 11 data sets of 78.7% (326,317 of 414,665) and timeliness of 41.1%; the document names the data sets and, for sentinel sites, health centres (CS) and general referral hospitals (HGR), not facility tiers as such, and does not say where reports are keyed.

ICTworks' July 2026 survey of national digital health strategies lists DR Congo's PNDIS II 2020-2024 as expired at the end of 2024, with PNDIS III not yet published; dated to the survey's publication.
